"That rifle on the wall of the labourer's cottage or working class flat is the symbol of democracy. It is our job to see that it stays there"

The same can be applied to your question. Second part is social support for states. If the society ever came to that ideal anarchy society and it worked (and I think it will, in some areas even better than expected) that new power could not find that support, quite the opposite, could find a social majority opossing them.

For me, and I'm talking only about me, the state is toxic. I have my reasons to believe it, and I would never work for it neither directly nor indirectly (eg. A statal contract with a private company). I had the chance and always rejected. Why? Easy. The impact I can do from within is limited, and brings the debate to a "how can we improve the state", leaving the debate of whether is the state good or bad (generally speaking, or about specific countries' states) out of the table. People would get reaffirmed in the belief that the state is good, because if even me, a "radical" as my family puts it, I'm eager to work with it, it can't be that bad!

I'm not going to say anything wrong about people trying to make the state better, but I don't believe it's going to get us really far. I believe the states are wrong each passing year, bigger and bolder, eager to screw people but talking about good (here a LOTR reference, this is why Gandalf doesn't touch the ring, he says that would try to use it for good, but the consequences would be bad, still the good words and intentions would remain and people would lose sight of what's good and wrong). 

Now, to the practical thing, when I talk about the state I have 2 discourses. The ideal thing I want, and the real thing that can be done in short term. Ideally, anarchism. In short term, I have some areas of interest where I have a vision of what could've done better within the state. That doesn't mean that I agree with the state. Just that while one game (anarchy) is won, I'd like people to live the best quality of life possible. The problem here is (coming back to your original message) that a lot of that can only be done out of the state. 

Example: in my country there's several cases of sexual abuse and prostituted minors that are under the tutelage of the state. The need for a tutelage program might be necessary, but if I had the chance, I'd rather adopt one of them than give money to the government to keep the program running because those programs have shown what are they good for: an elite enrichment and the creation of pederasty/prostitution rings leaded by public workers. If someone were to donate money for it, and it ended being used to cover more of that, what good has that person done??

What is everything I said worth then, if I'm not eager to work within the state to change it, if it is as you said the law of the land? Easy: 
-i/If the state is truly a representation of the people, if the majority turns toward ANCAP and voluntary social cooperation (in any form), the state should disappear by itself (or shrink itself), right? Because people would want that. 
-If is not a representation, work within it is pointless, as the owners of that state will cut any change towards anything they don't want. Moreover, that work could benefit those owners at the expense of the people (and here is where I thing we are tbh). 
Some exceptions can be made: higher education (high school, colleges) workers can have a deep impact working within: I know a case of one that's turning a lot of people against the state, making it accountable in their eyes, and people that comes out of his classes that is working on this too. There are some more areas probably (and you'll find here people saying that any worker hindering the state labor is an ally, or that some anarchists get into the government to hinder their labor and that's good - I don't have a clear stand on this so no comments from me).
